subject: Marginalizing imputed sample size (yea...): Am I doing it right?

messages.author: 2567ef0395c70306
messages.subject: Marginalizing imputed sample size (yea...): Am I doing it right?
parts:
I'm working on a meta analysis problem examining the effects of temperature on the decay rate of pathogens by incorporating reported time series of concentration and decimal reduction times from numerous studies in the literature. We're modeling the concentrations (C), including those associated with decimal reduction times, as mean estimates derived from samples of size S, with sample standard deviations sigma_C. Within the overall model, then, we account for the standard error of the mean concentrations using a normal distribution with scale parameter sigma_C/sqrt(S).

Many studies do not report either or both sigma_C or S, and so we have imputation models for these missing values. In the case of S, we use a negative binomial distribution fitted to the mean sample size of each study for which sample sizes were reported, with a multivariate normal prior on the mean and dispersion parameters. Since S is discrete, it must be marginalized to run the models in Stan (Since S essentially weights the influence of each observed concentration, I think we could also reasonably use a gamma distribution to calculate it, but I will need to learn to marginalize for a mixture model later on, so want to do this treating S as a discrete parameter).

The general model for observation i in experiment j in study L is

Ci ~ Normal ( μC0_j – Kj * ti  , σC_i / √SL )

μC0_j­­ ~ Normal ( C0_j , σC_i / √SL )

Kj ~ Normal ( K25 * eλ(T_j – 25) , σK )

K25 ~ HalfNormal ( μK25 , σK25 )

λ ~ Normal ( μλ , σλ )

μK25 ~ HalfNormal ( M2030 , Kscale )

μλ ~ Normal ( 0 ,  max( 1, ln( Kscale ) ) )

σK,σK25 ~ t ( 3 , 0 , Kscale )

σλ ~ t( 3 , 0 , max( 1, ln( Kscale ) ) )


Imputation Block


ln ( σC_i ) ~ Normal ( XT * β + μRes , σRes )


SL ~ Neg Binom ( μS , φS )


Β ~ MVNormal ( Meansβ , Σβ )


( μRes , σRes ) ~ MVNormal ( MeansRes , ΣRes )


( μS , φS ) ~ MVNormal ( MeansS , ΣS )

C, t ( time ), T_j, C0_j (initial concentration) , M2030, Kscale, XT (linear predictors for the standard deviation) and all the multivariate normal means and covariance matrices are provided as data.

In order to marginalize S, I was thinking that I could basically ignore everything (leave it as sampling statements in the model block) except for the normal density assigned to C, which drives the likelihood, μC0_j,and the binomial distribution on S itself. Is this correct? In which case, ignoring for the moment the different articulations of the variables at the level of experiment j and study L:

p(S, C|...) = Sum [over S = 2 to S=1000 (infinity, technically, but have to cap it somewhere)](

                                                                       Neg_binom_2(S | μS , φS) * Product [Over all imputed observations](
                                                                                                                                                                                         Integral[over μC0 = -Inf to Inf](
                                                                                                                                                                                                             Normal(μC0 | C0,σC / √S)*Normal(C|μC0-K*t , σC / √S)

Would that be more or less correct?

messages.author: 2567ef0395c70306
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Marginalizing imputed sample size (yea...): Am I doing it right?
parts:
So I've been puzzling about what to do with the dependence of the likelihood on both S and the value of μC0, which is also dependent on S. After some experimentation, it seems like I can incorporate both in the marginalization simply by putting an improper uniform prior (no prior) on μC0 and adding its normal probability density to the baseline negative binomial densities for each value of S. For example, for a single study with 30 observations in a single experiment:

transformed parameters{
vector[15] lps;
for (S in 1:15)
lps[S] = neg_binomial_2_lpmf( S | 2, 4)+normal_lpdf( μC0 | C0, sd_C0/sqrt(S) );
for (S in 1:15)
for (i in 1:30)
lps[S] = lps[S] + normal_lpdf( pts[i] | μC0-k * t[i], sd_Ci/sqrt(S) );

}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Marginalizing imputed sample size (yea...): Am I doing it right?
parts:
It helps to think generatively---that is,

* how the parameters arise from the priors (i.e., the prior distribution),
and then

* how the data arises from the parameters (i.e., the sampling distribution)

Viewed that way, you don't want to put the prior into the likelihood (which
is just the sampling distribution viewed as a function of the parameters for
fixed data)---the parameters are generated from the priors and then the
data generated from the parameters. The parameter generation comes first.
Having said that, you can sometimes blend them together with algebra to
get a faster evaluation of the joint density (prior * likelihood).

- Bob

messages.author: 2567ef0395c70306
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Marginalizing imputed sample size (yea...): Am I doing it right?
parts:
Hi Bob,

   In this situation, I have a discrete parameter that is used both in generating one of the parameters used to calculate the likelihood of the data, and in the likelihood for the data itself. Unless I'm mistaken, which is very plausible, the expression I wrote above is equivalent to evaluating the joint density of the data and parameter  μC0, the 'true' mean starting concentration / intercept.,for each potential value of the discrete parameter S. It's necessary in order to marginalize S out of both the likelihood of the data and the prior on μC0.

Philip

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Marginalizing imputed sample size (yea...): Am I doing it right?
parts:
That's not unusual. You see it in things like:

y ~ normal(mu, f(mu));

when you have a scale that depends on the location.
that doesn't cause any problems with the generative interpretation
of the models.

Now if there are infinitely many discrete values (or even a large
finite number), then you won't be able to use Stan unless there's
an analytic form of the marginalization.

- Bob
